title: James Cartlidge, Marc Dolgin, Christine Tomlinson - The Rise of the Roguelite
speaker: James Cartlidge, Marc Dolgin, Christine Tomlinson
description:
A fireside chat with the editor and coauthors of the upcoming academic book ‘The Rise of the Roguelite: Inside a Gaming Phenomenon’, forthcoming with Taylor and Francis/CRC Press. 

The book will be an edited collection of scholarly essays which explore roguelite games from a variety of disciplinary perspectives, including game design, narrative studies, philosophy, sociology, gender studies, and queer studies.

segments.text: So with all of that covered, I am excited to just get into our lovely speakers. This is
going to be fun. We have a fun set of talks for today. Without further ado,
I would like to bring on James Cartlidge to talk about an upcoming book, The Rise of the
Roguelite. It is an edited collection of scholarly essays exploring roguelite games from game design,
narrative studies, sociology, gender and queer studies. It will come out around
Christmas. I think it is right up the alley of the types of things we are interested in
here. We thought the preview event would be a great chance to talk about it. James
give you a chance to talk and we will bring on a couple coauthors in a bit.

ALEXEI: No, it is exciting and a cool opportunity to talk about here. We bring on a lot of

Is this an -- is there not a lot out there in terms of the roguelikes. How did you assembly this

Yeah, if we go around, Christine, if you go want to go first and talk about yourself and
your chapter, that would be great. >> Christine: Hello. I am Christine

Just how these games can be so different from each other and yet have some of

in the video game industry for many years and specializing mostly in roguelikes and

ALEXEI: I think we see that influence and working in Triple-A it has gone from being a roguelike

like that's a marketable skill now you reflect. Just to chat about the chapters on that topic,

>> I have spent time playing flash games and there is a lot of similarities and I have always wrote

and pegal roguelikes and so many more that I thought it was pretty important to just

ALEXEI: That's interesting. I saw, and I don't know who is putting the theory forward,

why say we like roguelikes. Yeah. Excellent. We will go this like queue style. Christine,
your chapter is about roguelites, romance, and the power of genre bending

You have this disparate game design approach of dating sim and visual novel style experience

ALEXEI: I would love to find out if that's true both in the sense if he was thinking about epic

a very powerful one that has a lot of -- well, through its interactivity, lots of possibilities

I like to do that kind of thing with games too. I think they offer such a rich potential
for conveying ideas and problematizing things and bringing out things you may not expect.
ALEXEI: I specialized in moral philosophy and here I am accidentally bringing that in
but I think the majority of certainly popular discussion around kind of philosophy and games

understanding them you have one more tool to try to think about the world. I think that is

ALEXEI: Marc, did you know what I am talking about?
>> Marc: I have heard of it but I don't know the details. Was hoping to hear more.

roguelikes and what they teach us? >> James: I almost wrote a chapter about

going to be that basically in -- the majority of like Triple-A games death means nothing because it

are literally talking about the same ideas in the world building because of this need to justify why
we have this infinite library of babble situation. I wonder if there is something to that too of now

the typewriter and all these questions that come from procedural generation and what does it mean

>> Marc: I have realized more and more there is two very distinct vibes or styles to roguelikes

much about explaining thing if everything isn't super serious. Even the biggest roguelikes ever

and you don't take things seriously, plays don't have to worry too much. But the moment you make
the game a little more serious than people want to get immersed and have reasons and explain why
am I starting over. Is it just because it is a video game and I have to start over? I think it
is interesting to see both approaches because I think there really is two different clans
in terms of the immersion of a game whether they want to try to actually explain why everything is
occurring or it is just a video game have fun. I find that to be interesting to see it and progress
more and more. I think there is more and more serious roguelikes occurring now that people
realize they can make a good engaging interesting story within a game that was just kind of like,

roguelike ties there. I think that's one that like, vague tonal spoilers, starts out funny
